parole.significato: -ery, making a business from a verb, e.g. baka (“to bake”) → bageri (“a bakery”)
parole.testo: From Low German -erie, from Old French -erie.
Borrowed from Low German aleke, alleke, further origin disputed. Cognate of Danish allike.
Borrowed from Low German also. Compare allt and så. Cognate to Norwegian Bokmål altså and Norwegian Nynorsk altso.
From Low German amme; compare with German Amme (“wet nurse”). Verb derived from noun.
Borrowed from Low German and German anbelangen. Compare Danish anbelange, Dutch aanbelangen.
Borrowing from older Low German Appelsina and in some dialects older Dutch appelsien. Equivalent to äpple (“apple”) + Kina (“China”).

parole.significato: to change (one worker for another), to relieve, to take over (for another person)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish aflösa, a calque of Low German aflösen or German ablösen, equivalent to av- + lösa.
Borrowed from Low German baviaan.
From Low German bal, bale, ultimately from the root of boll (“ball”).
From Low German bedoren, bedören. Equivalent to be- + dåra. Related to dåre (“fool”). Cognate with Danish bedåre, Norwegian Bokmål bedåre and German betören.
Borrowed from Low German behörich. Affix of be- + höra (“belong”) + -ig (“verb→adjective”). First attested in 1686.
Borrowed from Low German belammern. Cognate of Dutch belemmeren, German belämmern. Likely originally in the sense "paralyze", compare lam (“lame”).
From Low German beschieten. Equivalent of be- + skita.

parole.significato: only used in på eget bevåg
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German bewach, bewech (“deliberation”). Likely further influenced by våga (“dare”, verb), thus by surface analysis, be- (“en-”) + våga (“dare”). Cognate with German bewegen. First attested in 1620.
From Low German bicht(e). Compare Dutch biecht, German Beichte.

parole.significato: serious and hard; grim, stern, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German bister. Attested since 1665.

From Low German blick, from Middle Low German bleck, from Old Saxon *blek, from Proto-West Germanic *blik, from Proto-Germanic *bliką. Compare Danish blik (< Middle Low German bleck), German Blech (< Old High German bleh).
Borrowed from Low German blausel. Doublet of blå.
Since at least 1621, from braf (“good, brave”); from Low German brav; from French brave, borrowed from Italian bravo.
Borrowed from Low German brētling (“crucian carp; carp bream”). Cognate of German Breitling, Norwegian brisling, Faroese brislingur.

parole.significato: cot (simple bench to lie down on)
parole.testo: From Low German britsche, briske, from Low German bret (“board”). Attested since circa 1780. Cognate of German Pritsche, Danish brisk, Old High German britissa. Doublet of bräde.
From Low German bruk (“use”), from the verb bruken (“to use”).
From Low German bolt, from Middle Low German bolte, from Old Saxon bolt, from Proto-West Germanic *bolt.
Borrowed from Low German bums, imitative of a thud.

parole.significato: a (dense) collection of shrubs or bushes; a shrubbery or a thicket
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German buschkasche, from Old French boschage, from Vulgar Latin *boscāticum, from Latin boscus (“bush”), from Frankish *busk, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush; thicket”). First attested in 1658. Cognate with English boscage, Danish buskads, Norwegian Bokmål buskas, and

parole.significato: type of pullover blouse, originally worn by sailors, but now usually more loose-sitting and with a wide opening
parole.testo: From Low German buserun, busserun, from Dutch boezeroen, from French bourgeron. Compare Danish busseronne, Norwegian busserull.
Borrowed from Low German bülte, from Middle Low German bulte. Compare Dutch bult.
Borrowed from Low German bönhase, originally about artisans who were not members of a guild. Cognate of German Bönhase, Dutch beunhaas, Danish bønhas.

From Low German dis (“haze”), of West Germanic origin (compare Dutch dijs (“mist, fog”), West Frisian diish), of uncertain origin; possibly from Middle Low German dûnster, from Old Saxon *thinstar, from Proto-West Germanic *þimstr (“dusky, dark”). If so, related to modern Dutch deemster (“twilight”)
Borrowed from Low German dit un dat (“this and that”). Compare Norwegian ditt og datt.
Borrowed from Low German don (“"doing," work, thing”), from Low German don (“do”), which is cognate with English do, German tun.
Likely from Low German dragge. Cognate of Norwegian Nynorsk dregg, English drag.
Borrowed from Low German underduken (“dive down”). Doublet of ducka and dyka.
From Low German dörchdräven, from Old Saxon thurh + drivan. See also German durchtrieben, Danish durkdreven. Doublet of genomdriven.

parole.significato: eider, especially common eider, Somateria mollissima
parole.testo: From Low German eider, from Icelandic æður. Compare dialectal ära.

parole.significato: A godparent, or (more strictly) a godfather (person present at the christening who agrees to help raise the child)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish fadder, derived from Low German vadder, short for Low German gevadder, calque of Latin compater, affix of com- (“joint”) + pater (“father”). First attested in 1491.

parole.significato: a vane, a web (part of the anatomy of a bird's feather)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German fan, used since 1772, closely related to Swedish fana (“flag”).

parole.significato: to sweep, scrub, etc., and make nice and clean (a house or room or the like)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German clean and Borrowed from German fegen (“sweep, polish”). First attested in 1639.
Borrowed from Low German vinke (attested in the compound vinkenbür), likely a humorous form of Middle Low German venknisse. Cognate of German Gefängnis, Dutch gevangenis.

parole.significato: who works in a quick and accurate manner, able to do something very quickly yet still very accurately; nimble, deft
parole.testo: From Low German flink (“agile, quick”), probably from Middle Low German vlinken (“shining”). Perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *flakurōną (“to flutter, beat repeatedly”).
Borrowed from Low German flügg, flügge. Cognate of German flügge, Danish flyg. Compare Icelandic fleygur, Dutch vlug.

parole.significato: ridiculously small and insignificant, measly, paltry, petty
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German futtig, likely from Proto-Germanic *fuþiz.

Attested since the 13th century (Västgötalagen), from Old Swedish fangilse, fængilse, same construct as Old West Norse fangelsi, likely after Low German patterns. Equivalent to fånga + -else. Compare fängsla (“to imprison, to cuff”), fängsel (“imprisonment, cuffs”).
From Low German and Middle Low German vorbinden, from Old Saxon far- + bindan.
Borrowed from Low German vorkumpst. Related to verb förekomma via the same ending as in ankomst, hågkomst, härkomst, inkomst, uppkomst, åtkomst.

Originally from Low German vorsuffet in the past participle försoffad and meaning dismayed, disheartened. Later reinterpreted as för- (“en-, up”) + soffa (“couch”) + -ad (“-ed”) – "en-couch'd, couch'd up."

parole.significato: to entertain, to amuse, to divert
parole.testo: Calque of Low German vorstroien or German zerstreuen, itself a calque of French distraire (“to distract”), equivalent to för- + strö. Compare Danish adsprede, German verstreuen.

parole.significato: a curtain (in front of a window)
parole.testo: From Low German Gardine, from Early Modern Dutch gardine (contemporary Dutch gordijn), from French courtine, from Old French cortine, from Medieval Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”), from Latin cohors.
Inherited from Old Swedish gigha. Derived from Low German gige. Possibly derived from Old High German gigen (“rock, sway”). First attested in the latter 13th century.
Borrowing from Low German Gurk and German Gurke.
From Low German günnen, from Old Saxon giunnan, from Proto-Germanic *gaunnaną. See gunst and unna.

parole.significato: trade, commerce; the commercial exchange (buying and selling on domestic or international markets) of goods and services
parole.testo: From Low German handel, ultimately related to hand.

parole.significato: a cuckold (man with an unfaithful wife)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German hanerei, hanenrey (“cuckold; capon”). First attested in 1624. Compare with German Hahnrei, from the same source.

parole.significato: semla served in a bowl of hot milk
parole.testo: From Low German hetweggen, heetweggen pl, from Middle Low German hête weggen (“hot buns”); equivalent to het (“hot”) + vigg (“wedge”). Compare Danish hedevig, Norwegian heitevegg.

parole.significato: Acknowledging a mistake or expressing surprise; oops, whoops, oh
parole.testo: From Low German hopsa, related to Swedish hoppa (“to jump”).

Borrowed from Low German huller de buller. Compare Danish hulter til bulter, German holterdiepolter. Second half of phrase is from Middle Low German bulder and related to Swedish buller and German poltern. First half is likely a reduplication. Compare origin of English hurlyburly.
Derived from Low German fluckes. Doublet of flyga. Compare origin of huller om buller.
Borrowed through Low German hütte, from Old High German hutta.

parole.significato: to trim, to adjust, to clean up, to polish, to simplify
parole.testo: From either Low German *hüfschen or *höfschen, cognate of German hübschen (“make pretty”), from hübsch (“pretty”). Doublet of hövisk.
Borrowed from Low German hütt. First attested in 1839.

parole.significato: to detain awaiting trial; to remand
parole.testo: First attested in the 14th century (Magnus Erikssons landslag). From Old Swedish häkta, from Low German hechten, alternative form of heften. Cognate with häfta.
From Low German inbildsch (“haughty”), related to German einbildisch and German einbilderisch. See also Danish indbildsk.

Attested since 1529, from Low German jolle, from Middle Low German jolle, possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlos (“tube”), see also Lithuanian aulas, Norwegian aul, Hittite [script needed] (auli-, “tube-shaped organ in the neck”), Albanian hollë, Latin a

Borrowed from Low German cauwe, from Middle Low German kâ, from Old Saxon *kaha, from Proto-West Germanic *kahu, from Proto-Germanic *kawō (“jackdaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewH-. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kaie.
Borrowed from Low German kalkûn or Dutch kalkoen, nominalisation of kalkûnsche höner or kalkoensche haan "hen from Calicut" (modern Kozhikode, India). Doublet of kalikå.

parole.significato: a struggling for one's interests (often in opposition); a struggle, (sometimes more idiomatic) a fight
parole.testo: From Low German kempe, from Middle Low German kamp, from Latin campus (“battlefield”).

parole.significato: to heel to a position from which it is impossible to right one self; to founder
parole.testo: Attested since 1765; from Low German kantern with the same meaning; related to kant, "edge".

parole.significato: glue; substance used to make things stick, as a way of attaching a surface to another.
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish klisther, from Low German klīster, an originally Central German word, possibly from Old High German *klīstar, from Proto-West Germanic *klīstr, from Proto-Germanic *klīstrą (“paste, goo”), ultimately from the root of Klei (“clay”), from Proto-Indo-European *gleh₁y- (“to sm
Borrowed from Low German klüver or Dutch kluiver, from kluif. Cognate of German Klüver, Finnish klyyvari, Danish klyver.
From Low German knaphandig, superficially equivalent to knapp (“scarce”) + händig. Attested since 1827. Original meaning could have been connected to knapp in the now archaic sense "dexterous".
From Low German knode, knoden, corresponding to archaic German Knote (“coarse and uneducated man”).
From the verb kratta (“to rake, scratch”), from Low German kratten, probably from the same ultimate source as German kratzen (“to scratch”), which was borrowed into Danish kradse.

Borrowed from Low German krusedulle. The German word is a compound of two parts, the first part is related to German kraus (“curly”), the second part is of disputed origin. Compare Swedish krullidutt.

parole.significato: quince (the plant Cydonia oblonga or its fruit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German quiten, from Latin mālum cotōnium, from Ancient Greek μηλοκυδώνιον (mēlokudṓnion), from Κυδωνία (Kudōnía).
Borrowed from Low German kül.
Borrowed from Low German, but of uncertain origin outside of Germanic; see German Kegel (“pin, skittle”).
From Low German kempe; see kamp (“struggle”). Compare Danish kæmpe and Norwegian kjempe
Likely clipping of kökspiga. Compare origin of husa. Arguably from Low German köksche, from Middle Low German kokesche, from the noun koke (“kitchen”).
Borrowed from Low German loi, loie. Further origin disputed. Cognate of Danish løj, Dutch lui.

parole.significato: to a no longer attached or stuck state (no longer stuck to something, generally); loose, off, untied
parole.testo: From Low German los (“free, loose”), from Middle Low German lōs, from Old Saxon lōs, from Proto-West Germanic *laus. See also Danish los and Norwegian loss, Dutch loos. Doublet of lös.
Borrowed from Low German lukker, further origin uncertain. Cognate of German locker.
From a Low German word meaning "rag". Compare Dutch lomp, English lump, German Lumpen. First attested in 1855.

parole.significato: a trickster (one who fools or plays tricks or pranks on others)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German lūrfix. First part of compound related to lura (“deceive”), second part assumed to be related to German Fex.

From Low German leschen (“to extinguish”), from Middle Low German leschen, from Old Saxon leskan, from Proto-West Germanic *leskan. Related to modern Dutch lessen and modern German löschen. According to Svenska Akademiens ordbok the original meaning has been "to make something lay down" and related
From Low German manen, from Old Saxon manon, from Proto-Germanic *manōną, cognate with Old English manian (“to remind”).
From Low German manneke, manneken, diminutive of man. Doublet of mannekäng.
Borrowed through Low German, from Latin mil(l)ia (passum) "thousand (steps)." First attested in the latter half of the 14th century.

parole.significato: loose, slippery, partly melted snow, often mixed with mud
parole.testo: From Low German mode, from Middle Low German modder (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”).

parole.significato: to broker, to mediate, to negotiate (as a go-between)
parole.testo: From Low German mäkeln or mekelen, a frequentative of Middle Low German maken (see maka). Compare German makeln, mäkeln.
From Low German not, nut. Cognate with German Nut.

From Low German nück, nücke, from Middle Low German *nuken, from Old Saxon *hnukian, from Proto-West Germanic *hnukēn, ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *hnukāną (“to curve, be bent”). Compare Dutch nuk.
From Low German nemlik + -en

From Low German not, nut, from Proto-Germanic *hnōjaną (“to smooth, join together”), from Proto-Indo-European *kneh₂-. Cognate with Danish not, Norwegian Bokmål not, Norwegian Nynorsk not, nót and German Nut.

From Low German nat, naad, from Middle Low German nāt, from Old Saxon nād, from Proto-Germanic *nēdiz (“that which is sewn; seam; stitch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin (thread), to sew”). Cognate with Danish nåd, Norwegian Bokmål nat, Norwegian Nynorsk nat, German Naht and Dutch naa

parole.significato: A wide flat object, often solid and stiff, a plate
parole.testo: Derived from Low German platte or German platte. According to SO and SAOB attested since 1716.
Derived from Low German pliren. The German verb likely a mixup of two stems: piren (cognate with English peer) and blarren, blerren (cognate with English blear).

parole.significato: impose, force (something (undesirable) on someone, for example ideas)
parole.testo: From Low German düveln, from Low German Düvel (“devil”). Compare origin for dyvelsträck.
Probably from Low German pok (“child”), doublet of påk (“bludgeon”). Cf. archaic Danish pog.
Cognate of Danish regederlig. Likely from Low German regarderen. Compare French regarder.
Borrowed from Low German sipp. Attested since 1734.

parole.significato: to wear on (cause to be worn)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German schamfilen, likely variant of Middle Low German schamfēren.

parole.significato: to have the eyes turned in different directions, either deliberately (and temporarily) or due to strabismus
parole.testo: From Low German schelen, from Middle Low German schēle, from Old Saxon *skelh, from Proto-West Germanic *skelh (“squinting, crooked”).
From Low German schinke, from Middle Low German schinke, from Old Saxon skinka, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō. Cognate with English skink and Icelandic skinka.

parole.significato: a chimney (vertical tube or hollow column; a flue)
parole.testo: From Low German Schornstein, compound of schore (“support”) (ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skeran (“to cut”)) and Stein (“rock”) (from Middle Low German sten). Compare Danish skorsten and Norwegian Nynorsk skorstein.
From Low German shel, schele, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *skiljaną (“to divide, split”).
From Low German scherpe, probably from French écharpe, in which case from Old French escharpe.

sköld (“shield”) + padda (“toad”), from Old Swedish skioldpadda, a calque of Low German schildepadde, schiltpadde; compare with Norwegian Nynorsk skjelpadde, Danish skildpadde, Norwegian Bokmål skilpadde and Dutch schildpad. Compare German Schildkröte.
From Old Swedish skør, skyr, from Low German schör (“weak, fragile”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *skuriz, derived from the verb *skeraną (“to cut”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk skjør.
From Low German slagge, slakke, from Middle Low German slagge, perhaps from slagen (“to strike”), from Old Saxon slegi, from Proto-West Germanic *slagi.
From Low German and Middle Low German slange, from Old Saxon slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô.

parole.significato: to speak unclearly (due to poor articulation), to slur
parole.testo: From Low German sludern, from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Compare also Dutch slodderen (“to be sloppy”).

parole.significato: to stop (come to an end), to end (come to an end)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish slūta, from Low German sluten (“to lock up, shut”), from Middle Low German slūten, from Old Saxon *slūtan.
Borrowed from Low German smuggeln, from Middle Low German smugen, from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to slip through, creep”). Doublet of smyga.
Related to snut (“mouth”), also "snout," probably borrowed through Low German and ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *snūt.
Borrowed from Low German spitzbove. By surface analysis, spets + bov. Cognate of Dutch spitsboef, German Spitzbube.
Borrowed from Low German spölkumme. Cognate of Norwegian spilkum, Danish spølkum, Dutch spoelkom, German Spülkumm.

parole.significato: splice (to unite ropes by interweaving the strands)
parole.testo: Borrowed from either Low German splitsen or Dutch splitsen. Attested since 1741.

From Low German stickelber (“gooseberry”), the first element from Low German stickel (“tip, stinger”) (ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *stekan) and the second adapted to match Swedish bär (“berry”).

parole.significato: in starboard (right) direction of a vessel
parole.testo: From styra (“steer”) + bord (“bord, side of ship”), the side which the steering oar was located, i.e. right. Likely a calque of Low German stürbort. First attested in 1687.

parole.significato: jellied meat, head cheese (American English), brawn (British English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sylta, "to preserve; to salt", from Low German sülten, "boil in brine; preserve" and related to salt. The origin comes from the widespread use of salt as a preservative in pre-modern times.
synd + -a- + flod. Probably from Low German sintfluot. Compare Danish syndflod, German Sintflut, German Sündflut, Dutch zondvloed.

parole.significato: table (large and elongated table at a banquet or similar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German taffel or German Tafel. Doublet of tavla and tabell.

Inherited from Old Swedish talerk borrowed from Low German tallorken and Low German tallor, the latter possibly from Middle Dutch taeljoor (“cutting board, plate”) from Old French tailleor (“cutting board, plate”) from Old French tailler (“cutting off”) from Late Latin taliare (“cutting off”). Attes

parole.significato: science, scholarly knowledge, scholarship (collective discipline of learning acquired through any scholarly method; tot…
parole.testo: From Low German wetenskap, wetenschap, wetenschop, from weten (“to know”) + -schop (“-ship”), equivalent to veta + -skap. First attested in c. 1620. Compare Danish videnskab, Norwegian vitenskap, Dutch wetenschap, German Wissenschaft.

parole.significato: weight (what something weighs, measured in for example kilograms)
parole.testo: From Low German and Middle Low German wicht, from Old Saxon wiht, from Proto-West Germanic *wihti.

Either from German Gewehr, from Middle High German gewer, from Old High German giwerida or from Low German Gewehr. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål gevær, Danish gevær and Dutch geweer. Related to värja (“to defend, to protect”).

parole.significato: swerve, veer (quick turn to the side)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gier (“yaw”), from gieren (“to yaw”), or from the Low German equivalent.

parole.significato: A holiday, festival or similar festive occasion.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish höghtiþ with the same meaning (alternatively "wedding"), from Low German hochtid (“important religious or secular festivity”). Compare German Hochzeit (“wedding”).

Borrowed from Low German rēling, regeling or from Dutch reeling, regeling, from Middle Low German regel, from Old Saxon *rigil, probably borrowed from Latin regula (“bar, rule”). Cognate of German Reling, English railing, Danish ræling.
From Low German tuten, from Middle Low German tūten, either of imitative origin or derived from Proto-West Germanic *þeutan (“to howl”), itself probably imitative.
